clue.text: Constant interference

definitions.meaning: ... as an adjective means unchanging, steady
crackling noise that disrupts a radio signal

explanation.surface: Someone complains of never-ending meddling.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means fixed and unchanging, and is also the crackle of electrical noise spoiling reception.

clue.text: Little Welshman takes bird to bar at back of ship

indicators.note: little means the name is shortened, losing its last letter

parts.note: Taffy is a familiar nickname for a Welshman
the rail is a marsh bird

explanation.surface: A small man from Wales carries a bird into a pub at the stern of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' shortens the Welsh nickname by its last letter. 'Bar' looks like a pub, but here it is a handrail.
explanation.definitionFit: A taffrail is the handrail round a ship's stern.

clue.text: Chinese society about to raise an outcry in the W. Indies

indicators.note: about means the first piece goes round the next

parts.note: a triad is a Chinese secret criminal society

indicators.note: to raise in a down clue means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a din is a loud outcry or racket

explanation.surface: A gang is about to cause an uproar in the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is the container and 'to raise' turns the outcry upwards, as fits a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Trinidad is a Caribbean island, one of the West Indies.

clue.text: Hand over driving area to a body appointed for the purpose

definitions.text: a body appointed for the purpose

parts.note: to commit is to entrust or consign
a golfer drives off from the tee

explanation.surface: A golf course handed over to an official body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving area' suggests roads, but it is the golf tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A committee is a group of people appointed for a particular task.

clue.text: Sports event where place is in the bag

definitions.text: Sports event where place is in the bag

parts.words: Sports event where place is in the bag
parts.note: read as a contest where a finishing position is already assured; really a race run by children standing in sacks

explanation.surface: A competition whose result is a foregone conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the bag' is the idiom for a certainty, but here it is literal: the competitors hop along inside sacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A school sports-day race in which each runner stands inside a sack and hops to the line.

clue.text: Losing nothing by coming clean, not being susceptible to psychiatrists

definitions.meaning: describes fabric that keeps its size when washed
shrinks is slang for psychiatrists, so this reads as resisting them

explanation.surface: A confession costs nothing, and the patient will not respond to therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming clean' suggests confessing but means being washed; 'shrink' is slang for a psychiatrist.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth treated not to contract in the wash is so described, and the phrase literally means proof against psychiatrists.

clue.text: So-called have-not may be making some dough

indicators.note: so-called signals the word is as spoken, a sound-alike

parts.note: a have-not is a person in need, a needer

explanation.surface: A poor person might be earning some money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dough' suggests money, but it is bread dough, worked by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: One who works dough with the hands is making bread.

clue.text: Flier's body has a bearing on the case

indicators.note: on in a down clue means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: an air is a manner or bearing
a frame is a casing or surround

explanation.surface: The plane's fuselage affects the legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has a bearing on' reads as 'is relevant to', an idiom the setter splits into its separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: The airframe is the structure of an aircraft without its engines.

clue.text: Delicacy produced from cold storage

indicators.note: produced from means the following letters are made into something new

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A fine dish taken out of the freezer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produced from' rearranges C with STORAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Snails cooked in the French style are a gourmet treat.

clue.text: One who declares he will not swear

definitions.text: One who declares he will not swear

parts.words: One who declares he will not swear
parts.note: describes a witness who makes a solemn declaration in court instead of taking a religious oath

explanation.surface: A man refuses to use bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear' suggests cursing, but it means taking an oath; someone who declines the oath makes a solemn affirmation instead.
explanation.definitionFit: In court a person may affirm rather than swear on a holy book, and such a person is so named.

clue.text: It's a mile to James Hogg's place, say — that sort of measurement

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for mile

indicators.note: say tells us the place name is taken by its spoken sound, not its spelling

parts.note: the poet James Hogg was known as the Ettrick Shepherd, from Ettrick in the Scottish Borders

explanation.surface: A traveller notes the distance to a Scottish poet's home, then speaks of measuring systems.
explanation.walkthrough: James Hogg (1770-1835) was the 'Ettrick Shepherd'; ETTRICK is a valley in the Scottish Borders. 'Say' turns its sound into ETRIC, and 'It's a mile to' puts M in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The system of metres and kilograms is a kind of measurement, so a measure of that kind is described this way.

clue.text: The production of oranges, perhaps, for enjoyment

definitions.meaning: read as fruit plus -ion, the bearing of fruit, with oranges as an example
an old sense of the word is pleasure from possessing something

explanation.surface: Growing citrus fruit for the pleasure of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual modern meaning, realisation of a plan, is not used; both senses here are the literal bearing of fruit and the archaic sense of enjoyment.
explanation.definitionFit: The word literally means fruiting, and in older English meant the pleasure of possession or use.

clue.text: A king holding sceptre the wrong way — he's in love!

indicators.note: holding means the first pieces grip the next one between them

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, here simply a royal abbreviation for a monarch

indicators.note: the wrong way means the rod is read backwards

parts.note: a sceptre is a ceremonial rod

explanation.surface: A monarch clutches his staff of office upside down while lovestruck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's in love' is the whole definition; 'the wrong way' turns the rod round and 'holding' places it inside 'A king'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who worships another is a lover, a person in love.

clue.text: Near-riot breaking out at the front

indicators.note: breaking out suggests disorder, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Trouble is brewing among those standing in the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking out' rearranges the eight letters of NEAR-RIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Anterior is the anatomical and formal word for placed forward, in front.

clue.text: The French ship on the Douro foundering without trace

indicators.note: a foundering ship breaks up, so the river's name is broken up and rearranged

parts.note: le is the French masculine for the
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A French vessel sinks on the Portuguese river without leaving a sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The Douro is a river in Spain and Portugal. 'Foundering' rearranges it to ODOUR, followed by LE and SS.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no smell means leaving no scent trace behind.

clue.text: Swung round forcibly, we got thrown out of vehicle

indicators.note: got thrown out of means the letters of we are removed from the longer word

parts.note: to slew is to turn or swing violently round

explanation.surface: Two passengers are ejected when a car spins violently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got thrown out of' takes WE away from SLEWED, leaving SLED.
explanation.definitionFit: A sledge or sleigh is a vehicle on runners for snow.

clue.text: Thin bone meal

parts.note: spare means lean or thin
a rib is a bone

explanation.surface: A lean bit of bone served as a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare ribs, pork ribs with little meat, make a dish.

clue.text: Thomas Arnold, for example, a man of strict justice, cut up rough

indicators.note: cut means the second piece slices into the first
up in a down clue means the word is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: rude means rough or crude
Cato the Censor was the Roman proverbial for rigid moral severity

explanation.surface: A Victorian headmaster, a stern moralist, became angry.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arnold was the famous headmaster of Rugby School. 'Up' reverses RUDE to EDUR; 'cut' has CATO slice into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A headmaster is an example of a teacher, someone who educates.

clue.text: Splinter group in school

definitions.meaning: a breakaway faction from a larger religion or party
a school of thought, a group following one doctrine

explanation.surface: A breakaway faction forms in a classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is not a place of lessons but a school of thought.
explanation.definitionFit: A sect is a breakaway religious group and also a body of followers of one teaching.

clue.text: Notice handicapped miler is getting fitter

parts.note: to see is to notice

indicators.note: handicapped means the runner's word is disabled, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A runner with a disability is spotted getting into better shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitter' looks like healthier but means more fitting, more proper; 'handicapped' jumbles the runner's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Seemly means proper or becoming, so the comparative means more appropriate.

clue.text: Astonishing people to listen to, these waterproofers!

indicators.note: to listen to means the word is judged by ear

parts.note: a corker is a remarkable, astonishing person or thing

explanation.surface: Sealers of ship seams are remarkable people to hear.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech CORKERS and the answer sound alike; 'corker' is British slang for someone striking.
explanation.definitionFit: They seal seams in boats or windows against water with a filler.

clue.text: The mainspring of such cops

definitions.meaning: the central principle on which everything else depends
the ... Cops were the bungling policemen of silent film comedies

explanation.surface: A remark about what drives a certain kind of policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mainspring' suggests a watch, but it means the central principle; the silent-film Keystone Cops give the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The central stone of an arch holds it together, hence the essential principle; silent comedies featured incompetent policemen of that name.

clue.text: Punt not available for a start

parts.note: a punt is a kick of the ball dropped from the hands
off means not on the menu, unavailable

explanation.surface: A boat can't be hired to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punt' suggests a flat-bottomed boat, but it is a kind of kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A football match begins with the opening kick, so it is a beginning.

clue.text: Style of architecture in Morocco, perhaps, away from the capital

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the remaining letters are just one possible arrangement, so they are shuffled
away from the capital means the capital letter at the head of the word is dropped

explanation.surface: An ornate building style found in North Africa outside Rabat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The capital' looks like Rabat, but it is the capital letter M. Dropping it leaves OROCCO, which 'perhaps' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Rococo is the florid eighteenth-century decorative style that followed Baroque.

clue.text: Proceed hurriedly, and jumble one's words

definitions.meaning: to move or climb in a rush
to mix up a message so it cannot be understood

explanation.surface: Someone rushes and stumbles over their speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To scramble is to hurry or clamber, and to garble a message so it is unintelligible.

clue.text: You will need some corroboration to get the dole

indicators.note: some means only part of the word is taken, the run inside it

explanation.surface: A benefits claimant must provide evidence to receive payments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The dole' suggests unemployment benefit, but dole here is an allotted share.
explanation.definitionFit: A dole is a portion handed out, an allowance of food or goods.

clue.text: American fishes from lake with sea view perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could be arranged differently, so they are shuffled

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Fish caught in the US from a lakeside spot overlooking the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges L with the letters of SEA VIEW.
explanation.definitionFit: The alewife is a North American herring-like fish, so several are fishes of that kind.

clue.text: Convey by word of mouth the infantry are excused boots!

indicators.note: by word of mouth means the word is taken as heard, not spelt

parts.note: to bear is to carry or convey
foot soldiers are the infantry, so foot means infantry

explanation.surface: A message is passed on orally that soldiers no longer need to wear boots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By word of mouth' acts only on the verb for convey; the infantry is added as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone let off wearing boots goes with nothing on their feet, unshod.

clue.text: Pressure for closure of Thames lock

indicators.note: closure of means the closing letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: a lock of hair is a tress

explanation.surface: Strain on the system forces a river lock on the Thames to be shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' looks like a canal lock but is a lock of hair; 'closure of' takes the S that ends Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress is strain or pressure on something.
